events.title: Anthropic's Amodei says China presents 'toughest dilemma' for his proposed AI slowdown
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the "toughest dilemma" about his proposal to slow the advancement of AI is what happens if China does not do the same. Amodei published an essay on Saturday urging AI companies to slow how quickly they improve their most advanced models. The essay landed during a pivotal time for the AI industry, which is facing public backlash over its data centers and comes amid former-Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon's warning about the threat to humanity. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said Sunday that the "toughest dilemma" about his proposal to slow the advancement of artificial intelligence is what happens if adversarial nations, namely China, choose not to do the same. "The more long-term thing would be working together to put a speed limit on the rate of of AI progress," Amodei told CBS News' "Sunday Morning." "I think that's going to be very difficult because the incentives to pull ahead and the military advantage that you get from that are so large. And honestly, I don't know if it's possible, but we should we should try." Amodei published an essay on Saturday urging AI companies to slow how quickly they improve their most advanced models, a move that followed stark warnings from industry researchers last week about the technology's growing potential to cause catastrophic harm. An Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon , announced he quit his job out of concern that the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI , are " gambling with our lives ." In recent months, AI models from Chinese startups have gained steam against leading offerings from American companies like OpenAI and Anthropic , sparking concern from lawmakers and experts in Silicon Valley. Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sunday called for a "consensus-based global AI governance framework" at the BRICS bloc summit in India and said China will help establish a BRICS AI open-source community . BRICS held its inaugural summit in 2009 and is now made up of 11 nations, including China, India, Russia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates. President Donald Trump is slated to meet with Xi at the White House on Sept. 24, and the two leaders are expected to discuss AI. Amodei's essay landed during a pivotal time for the AI industry, which is facing public backlash over its data centers and mounting calls for regulation out of Washington. Anthropic and OpenAI are also gearing up for potentially historic IPOs , though neither company has set an official date for a debut. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Saturday that the company will likely not go public this year, in part because of concerns around safety. "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," Altman said in an interview with Fortune . Altman's relationship with Amodei, who defected from OpenAI to start Anthropic, has been strained in recent years. But Altman expressed support for Amodei's essay in a post on X on Saturday, writing that he agrees on the need to "pace the frontier." Several other industry leaders, including Demis Hassabis, the chair of Google DeepMind, and Elon Musk , CEO of both Tesla and SpaceX , also welcomed Amodei's proposal. "Dario's essay points towards the right path forward," Hassabis wrote in a post on X on Saturday. "The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment." Apple event live updates: First foldable iPhone, new watch series expected as Ternus makes debut Andreessen- and Thiel-backed defense startup opens U.S. missile factory as it exits stealth Anthropic researcher says AI has more than 10% chance of 'killing all humans' after colleague quits How one hedge-fund manager built his firm to be powered entirely by AI agents In the essay, Amodei proposed a three-step plan aimed at slowing the pace of development without "sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI." Amodei said Anthropic has "unilaterally" committed to the first step of the plan, which grants third-party evaluators employee-level access to the company to verify safety practices and report incidents. The second step encourages leading AI companies within democratic countries to coordinate and establish common safety standards, and the third calls for coordination between democratic governments and authoritarian governments. "Dario is right that there should be some oversight," Musk wrote in a post on X early Sunday morning. "Peer review of AI by competitors is the right way to start this off." Musk, who has for years warned about the potential risks of AI, was quick to express support for Amodei on Saturday. He had been a major critic of Anthropic until his rocket company SpaceX, which acquired his AI startup xAI earlier this year, inked a major compute deal with the company in May. As part of the deal, Anthropic will pay SpaceX $1.25 billion per month through May 2029, according to filings. "Everyone I met was highly competent and cared a great deal about doing the right thing," Musk wrote following the deal.

events.title: The Guardian view on the government’s corporate reforms: entrenching neoliberalism, not ending it | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on the government’s corporate reforms: entrenching neoliberalism, not ending it A recent consultation on corporate reporting prizes the interests of shareholders over society. It’s a step in the wrong direction T he question of what corporations are for is deeply political. In a 1970 article for the New York Times, Milton Friedman argued that the “social responsibility of business is to increase its profits”. The idea that CEOs should worry about providing good jobs was “pure and unadulterated socialism”, he wrote. Friedman and his fellow neoliberals saw companies as vehicles for enforcing their politics. Their ideas endured: UK bosses are now paid 130 times more than average workers. Despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism, a 12-week consultation recently launched by his government risks entrenching it. The consultation was first announced as part of the Starmer government’s crusade against “red tape”. The average annual report for some businesses now runs to 98,000 words, and no doubt there are areas that could be simplified. But the consultation proposes removing vital information and presumes that company reports primarily serve shareholders, rather than other stakeholders. Both are steps in the wrong direction. The consultation proposes scrapping information about the ratio between CEO and worker pay, removing a vital benchmark for inequality. British CEOs already earn 95% more on average than their European equivalents, and opaque pay ratios only serve their interests. There is scant evidence that higher-paid CEOs create more productive firms. As one Harvard Law School paper observed, pay ratios show how much a company invests in its “human capital”, and matter to workers and investors alike. Consumers who are made aware of this information are more likely to choose products from firms where the ratio is lower, encouraging those firms to address glaring pay disparities. The consultation reflects the idea that inequality within a company is immaterial, a perplexing stance for a government concerned with fairness. It suggests removing annual shareholder votes on director pay, on the basis that votes are still required every three years. Annual votes were a modest attempt from Theresa May’s Tory government to tame the “unacceptable face of capitalism”, and the GC100 lobby group of corporate leaders has called to scrap them. By giving way, Labour would be removing a Tory policy designed to rein in boardroom greed. It also proposes allowing companies to shift towards fully virtual annual general meetings. Companies have been holding online AGMs since Covid, and the government suggests these can improve “accessibility”. This is misguided: such meetings tend to be shorter, and prevent shareholders from asking as many questions. In-person AGMs are an imperfect form of accountability, but confrontation is easier to avoid when people aren’t in the room. Earlier this year, more than 50% of BP shareholders voted against a resolution to replace in-person AGMs with online meetings. Shareholders and climate groups argued these were a threat to accountability . If reporting is too onerous, it would be better to start afresh with a new regime that recognised the interests of workers and society at large. Some voluntary initiatives, such as B Corporations , already take a more holistic approach to the information they disclose. Even better would be a requirement to include workers on company boards and provide greater transparency on pay levels, including that of all executives and workers paid less than the living wage. As the legal professor Katharina Pistor observes, corporate law is a tool that creates inequality. If the government wants to end neoliberalism, it should scrap this consultation and start again.

events.title: Johnson calls for AI solutions but says Congress won't take the lead
events.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Sunday that Congress won't lead the charge on regulating AI safety . Why it matters: Calls for AI companies to adopt safety protocols reached a fever pitch this week, prompting the four biggest AI labs to endorse slowing their models' development. Driving the news: Johnson was urged this week to cancel the House recess and bring representatives back to D.C. to pass a law on AI safeguards. During a Sunday appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," Johnson said Congress intervening isn't the answer and that AI companies can halt their work at any time. We have to "resist Congress jumping in and imposing some sort of emergency moratorium. It's got to be done right, safely, wisely. In a separate appearance on NBC's "Meet the Press," Johnson conceded that he would recall House members and schedule a vote on AI regulation "if we had a solution," but said any action from Congress must be done carefully. "We have to put up some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn't run away ....But at the same time, we've got to make sure that we don't lose our edge in the global competition on this with China. Because that would be a national security threat." What they're saying: Johnson told CNN and NBC he would like to organize a meeting between President Trump , members of Congress, and the top AI officials who call the shots at their respective companies. Johnson added to CNN that he would prefer AI company leaders to take a leadership role and responsibility for ensuring the safety of their products, rather than pushing Congress to implement rules. Johnson's comments mirror former White House AI czar David Sacks, who said late Saturday that the major labs should simply pace development on their own, without the government having to intervene. The other side: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told ABC's "This Week" that Democrats planned to meet Tuesday morning to discuss AI. "We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down, as the CEOs have recently acknowledged, slow down the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely," he said. Zoom out: CNN's Jake Tapper pointed out that several AI leaders agreed with a 3,800-word essay published Saturday by Anthropic's Dario Amodei, in which he proposed slowing AI development and implementing more safety measures. Johnson seemed skeptical, saying that the companies "all have very different ideas on what the guardrails should be. There's no consensus among them. And Congress is obviously less qualified than the people who are pushing this frontier to know all the ins and outs of it." The House speaker also said Americans shouldn't panic over the technology and the doomsday warnings , though Axios' Andrew Solender reported last week that rank-and-file members of Congress are urging action . "We need to handle this new technology like we have others in the past and make sure we're doing everything we can responsibly to also not smother American innovation. We have to do both things simultaneously," Johnson said. Under the partnership, Lyft handles fleet services, such as vehicle readiness and maintenance, as well as infrastructure and depot operations through its wholly owned subsidiary Flexdrive. In Nashville, customers can hail a Waymo robotaxi directly from the Waymo app, or try their luck on the Lyft app, which will match riders with a Waymo depending on availability. Lyft has more than dabbled in autonomous vehicle technology over the years, including through partnerships with Aptiv (now Motional) in Las Vegas, May Mobility in Atlanta, Baidu in London, and Waymo in Phoenix . But this week is notable because it marks Lyft’s first true entry into commercial robotaxi services using driverless vehicles without a human operator behind the wheel. Lest you forget, the company spent four years and millions of dollars developing its own AV tech under its Level 5 business division. Lyft sold its autonomous vehicle unit to Toyota’s Woven Planet Holdings subsidiary for $550 million in 2021 — one of many acquisitions during a period of widespread consolidation across the nascent industry. Lyft then took a break from AVs as it focused on its core ride-hailing business. But it didn’t dismiss the idea altogether. I spoke to Jeremy Bird , Lyft’s executive vice president of growth, about the milestone and thought I would share a few insights. In his role, Bird manages Lyft’s international, luxury, and autonomous vehicle plans — and sometimes all three may converge. When I asked Bird when we’ll see more robotaxis on the Lyft app — and where — he didn’t get too specific. But he did say the company went into 2026 focused on its partnership with Waymo in Nashville and Baidu in London (where commercial service has not yet launched). “I think next year what you’ll see is more diversification of that,” he said, adding that ideally this would include expanding Lyft’s partnership with both partners. “I think next year will be a big year for us.” And it seems international markets are a big part of that AV expansion plan. Bird called London a “fascinating market,” and throughout our conversation he repeatedly talked about Lyft as a global company, a notable shift from just a few years ago when it was focused on the U.S. market. So, where is Lyft headed next? When it comes to international markets, Lyft seems to be prioritizing locations where it can operate a hybrid network — meaning AVs and human-driven vehicles — from the get-go. “We are a global company becoming more global, which is important for us,” he said. “And AVs will be the way we think about the future. Like any market we go into, is there an AV component to that? Is it a market where AVs are already open regulatorily, or that would put that market up higher on our list of the places we want to go?” A little bird noticed a couple of interesting hires over at Ford that sure look like the company is building up its defense tech muscles. Ford recently hired ex-Raytheon employee Tomaz Seignemartin as VP of continuous improvement and former General Dynamics staffer Shirish Srinivasan, who is now chief of staff to Ford’s chief strategy officer. Ford also hired Nathan Rigoni, who was Lockheed Martin’s generative AI team lead, as senior software engineer. Now, of course, a handful of defense tech hires at a company that employs thousands is hardly a trend. But it does illustrate how having a background in defense tech has become more valuable. Got a tip for us? Email Kirsten Korosec at kirsten.korosec@techcrunch.com or my Signal at kkorosec.07, or email Sean O’Kane at sean.okane@techcrunch.com . The Boring Company , the startup founded by Elon Musk to “solve traffic” by creating a network of underground tunnels, raised $3 billion in a round led by the United Arab Emirates. The Boring Company is now valued at $23 billion, the company shared in its announcement. There is a reason for UAE’s support. The Boring Company, which already worked with the UAE on the Dubai Loop, said it will dig another 150 kilometers of tunnels in the Middle Eastern country. Andreessen Horowitz, Sequoia Capital, Human Capital, Vy Capital, and Valor Equity Partners also participated. In the U.S., the Boring Company’s most visible work is in Las Vegas, where it has developed tunnels connecting hotel casinos such as Resorts World, Encore, and the Sahara, the convention center, and limited trips to the airport. Tesla vehicles, driven by a human, shuttle riders to and from these locations.

events.title: My partner and I split our lives between the US and Canada — and have no plans to pick just one place
events.summary: I feel like I can enjoy the best parts of the US and Canada. Catherine Collins My partner lives in Canada , and I'm in the US — and neither of us has immediate plans to move. Spending time in both places lets me enjoy my favorite parts of both American and Canadian culture. In the future, we've discussed living in Canada for half the year and spending winters in the US. For a week every month, I take a two-and-a-half-hour flight from Chicago to Winnipeg, Canada. That might sound surprising: It's a lot of time to spend in the air, and Chicago has so much to offer. However, I've been in a long-distance relationship with my Canadian partner, Andrew, for over two years, and neither of us is ready to move just yet. Andrew and I met at a conference for financial bloggers a decade ago, and we were great friends and colleagues for many years before we became a couple. Today, we run an online business together , which allows us to work remotely and travel regularly between our countries. Because we both have children from previous marriages, neither of us plans to move countries anytime soon. There are challenges, but I feel like I get the best of both worlds In my experience, Canada has a more relaxed pace. Catherine Collins As an American, I've gotten used to certain apps, tools, and conveniences that I can't access in Canada. For example, Canada doesn't have Venmo or Cash App, so Andrew and I split costs or pay each other back using Wise. If we start a movie on Hulu, we can only watch it when we're in the States, since the streaming service isn't available in Canada. As inconvenient as that can be, I often feel like I get the best of both worlds. Take food, for instance: Andrew looks forward to getting Chick-fil-A when he visits me, because there isn't a location in Winnipeg. (Although the chain does exist in some bigger Canadian cities, like Toronto.) And, though we have A&W here in the US, it doesn't have poutine on the menu, which is the unofficial Canadian national dish . So, I always make sure to order that when I visit him. I've found that the pace and culture feel very different in both places, too. As someone who's been self-employed for almost 15 years, I appreciate being able to surround myself with other motivated entrepreneurs whenever I'm here. In Winnipeg and other Canadian cities I've visited, though, I've been able to slow down more. The pace feels more relaxed, and I often think of Canada as my safe haven. In the future, we might choose both We've talked about spending half the year in Canada. Catherine Collins There are also structural differences between the two places. Canadians fund their universal healthcare system through taxes, whereas a majority of Americans have private insurance . What's nice about Canada's system is that residents don't have to stress about an unexpected bill or an expensive ER visit. That said, there can be trade-offs, like longer wait times for emergency care and surgeries. In the US, I appreciate that I can usually make medical appointments quickly, even though they come at a cost. There are parts of American culture that will always feel hard to leave, but spending so much time in Canada has also shown me that stepping away from hustle culture can be soothing for my soul. There are parts of American life that Andrew appreciates, too — but I know that if we live elsewhere, he'll miss many aspects of his home, like his close-knit family and the beautiful, wide-open prairies in Winnipeg. I'm not sure what the future holds once all our kids go to college, but we will likely spend half the year in Canada and then work remotely in a warmer area during the winter. Whatever we choose, I know what will matter most is making sure we create a lifestyle that feels unique to us, a perfect blend of our cultures together. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC
events.summary: 'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AI An artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic has said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity. "I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said. Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry. The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, recently called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this. The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development. Amodei wrote in an essay on Saturday that developing the technology was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious", and that companies and governments must be given time to address them. Coxon – who worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic – welcomed the suggestion of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China to avoid "a race at an international scale". "The people who work at these companies are completely serious when they ask for regulation because they find themselves trapped in a race. And they're scared of the outcomes of that race," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down Published 1 day ago The hardest question to answer, according to Coxon, was what an AI apocalypse would look like. One of the risks outlined in Amodei's comments was of a swarm of bots acting like a supercomputer that could take over the internet. Coxon said this scenario could be realistic in six months to a year. In response to Coxon's departure, an Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News: "We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. "To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry." The firm has been a pioneer in studying how AI models work, the spokesperson added. It was the first to publish a framework for mitigating the risks posed by their development - and it also "aggressively" tests its models and publishes the findings to aid scrutiny and prevent incidents of "AI misalignment". "This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models," they said. Coxon said his peers feared the danger could even arrive in the next two years. He said staff at AI firms were "planning what to do with their lives and thinking about the impacts of their work", while some were "considering buying land somewhere because they're so scared of the instability as a result of rapid AI progress". "They all keep this in their head on a daily basis while working on the technology." But Coxon did have some optimism about the future of AI, telling the BBC that the people researching the technology "genuinely want to see the upside" of things like "solving diseases and improving everyone's lives". Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans' Published 4 days ago Many others in the industry have also voiced their concerns since Coxon's social media post, including Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger . "We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger said. Computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC on Friday that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans was "not unreasonable" , external . Meanwhile, Marc Warner, chief executive of AI safety firm Faculty, told the BBC's The World This Weekend that it was "extremely hard to place a probability" on AI killing all humans. "But it's important to recognise that these people are very sincere in what they're saying," he added, noting that the risks surrounding AI have been raised by the heads of several AI firms for years. Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, who is a paid adviser to Anthropic, wrote in the Sunday Times , external that he too was worried about the risk of AI to humanity despite generally being optimistic. Dramatic insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley Published 23 hours ago However, some industry figures have suggested comments are overstated or may be designed to generate hype. Chief executive of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, said on social media: "Sorry, but asking Jacob [Coxon] about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change.

events.title: The AI doomsday debate has reached a boiling point
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei have called for a slowdown in AI. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images, FABRICE COFFRINI/AFP via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Existential angst What do you do if you feel like you're helping build something that could contribute to the end of humanity? This is the existential question confronting the AI industry, a debate that only intensified after Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit last week with a stark warning . He said AI giants are "gambling with our lives" and that the people building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." The swift reaction to Coxon's warning boiled over on Saturday when the leaders of the biggest AI companies publicly agreed on what should happen next. In a Saturday essay, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says he's "become convinced" the breakneck pace of advancement must change and proposed a three-step solution to ensure the tech's safety. Shortly afterward, Elon Musk and Sam Altman publicly aligned with Amodei's plan in a rare sign of support. "Dario is right," Musk tweeted. Altman agreed, too, saying the pace of development has been a "primary topic" of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks. Altman also said OpenAI might not move forward with an IPO this year. "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," he said in a Fortune interview. As fears over AI safety intensify, employees at Anthropic and OpenAI have also been speaking out. My colleague Sarah Needleman reported on a big question facing many concerned AI employees : Should they quit or stay amid fears of an AI apocalypse? Some AI workers believe they can do more good by staying on the inside. That means raising concerns, pushing for safeguards, and trying to influence decisions before they are made. Others worry that staying at these companies only helps legitimize a race that some believe is getting dangerously out of control. BI's Alistair Bar explored some of these theories in this week's edition of AI Insider — you can subscribe here to his weekly newsletter. Are employees at the big AI lab companies better off leaving or staying if they feel like their work is contributing to a possible AI apocalypse? Send me a note at srussolillo@businessinsider.com and let me know what you think. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: My husband and I were college athletes. We're not pushing competitive sports on our kids.
events.summary: The author (right) and her husband were both college athletes. Courtesy of Rachel Morgan Cautero. My husband and I were both college athletes who love sports. We're not pushing our kids to specialize in a sport early and encourage other activities. We want to avoid injuries and burnout while allowing them to explore their own interests. My husband and I were both college athletes . When we had two boys, I think people naturally assumed we'd push the sports route hard. After all, I was a four-year starter on my college soccer team, while my husband played football for an Ivy League college. But we've actually taken the opposite approach, and in addition to the expected soccer, baseball, and flag football dalliances, many of my kids' activities are non-sports-related. Think piano, musical theater, and Cub Scouts. Our kids are 6 and 8, and we're not pushing sports on them right now. Here's why. We want them to be well-rounded Kids around us are engaging in competitive sports earlier and earlier. Hospital for Special Surgery, citing the National Council of Youth Sports , reports that about 27% of the 60 million children and teens who participate in organized sports each year play only one sport. These kids are often practicing year-round, competing on travel teams, and in some cases, playing on multiple teams for the same sport. While parents' intentions are good — their kid loves a sport, they're good at it, why not encourage it? — research has shown that there's not always a clear benefit to early sports specialization, or ESS. Instead, I've read that it could be detrimental to kids' sports success, as it can lead to overuse injuries and burnout, and may actually  impede overall motor development . Do you have a hot take on a common parenting belief? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. Free play is a priority for us One of the rules we have in our home is that each kid can play one sport per season . With two kids, we have practice at most twice a week and games on Saturdays. That leaves lots of time for free play. Studies have shown that unstructured play is immensely important to kids' developing brains, but it is being summarily replaced by youth sports and its demands. I consider it a win that with two kids, I'm able to reserve three afternoons a week solely for free play . Will that change if they choose to embrace travel sports? Sure. But for now, they make up elaborate games with their neighborhood friends, ride their bikes and scooters, and honestly, make the biggest messes, both inside and out. We want to avoid injuries and burnout My laundry list of soccer-related injuries is long. I've had countless sprained ankles, a broken nose, a badly hyperextended elbow, chipped teeth, and torn ligaments in both my knees, one of which resulted in surgery. My husband suffered two concussions, which ended his collegiate career. The author said her husband suffered two concussions while playing college football, ending his playing career. Courtesy of Rachel Morgan Cautero. Early sports specialization (ESS) is a surefire way to increase the risk of overuse injuries. At this stage, I'll do just about anything to avoid the ER, including putting off competitive sports . With two boys, we're already frequent fliers. We also don't want them to burn out. As seasoned athletes, we know what it's like to burn out, and we don't want the same for our kids. After sitting in school for 7 hours a day, we want them to choose extracurriculars that truly light them up, speak to their passions, and are, well, fun. That means that sometimes it's flag football, and sometimes it's ukulele lessons. Both are equally valuable. We're taking a thoughtful approach Both my kids play baseball , but with a few caveats. Both are playing on an official Little League team, which means fields are uniform, playing time is mandated, and there are limits on things like the number of pitches allowed per day. We don't require them to practice on their own time, unless they want to. We do require them to finish the season if they sign up to play on a team, but we don't require them to sign up for any sport again if they truly don't like or enjoy it. It sounds random, but it seems I've modeled my philosophy after the Norwegian approach to youth sports. This was brought to my attention after the recent Winter Olympics . In short, Norwegians prioritize joy over winning, don't keep score until kids are older, and don't allow ESS. The result is a country that boasts a record of 447 Winter Olympic medals (including 166 gold), an impressive soccer team (hello, Erling Haaland, who we all enjoyed during the World Cup), and many other elite athletes — all without pressuring children to excel in sports early. But don't get me wrong. I'm not anti-sports. Playing soccer for most of my life gave me so much — a work ethic, lifelong friends, a sense of belonging, and a sense of responsibility to the greater good. But sports aren't the only way to learn those skills, and I won't freak out if my children choose not to pursue the college sports route. At the end of the day, all I want is for them to be happy, well-rounded kids. And if that means playing sports, great. If not, that's OK, too. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A joyful harvest: the young Welsh farmers growing food for Birmingham
events.summary: A charity in Powys provides the land while growers do the hard work, producing bumper crops for city children Kilos and kilos of courgettes, cucumbers, tomatoes and salad leaves are ripe and ready for picking on a small Welsh farm in the rural county of Powys. The haul being harvested by Tilly Gomersall is not just impressive after a difficult growing season hit by a record string of heatwaves and drought across all of Wales and most of England, but all the more remarkable given that 18 months ago the site was uncultivated pasture. “Until now, I’ve just been turning the earth with my own power,” Gomersall says. “We’ve got a two-wheel tractor, but you do have to heft that around with your body quite a lot and we’re cultivating from pasture, so it’s really hard work.” The site at Wern farm, near Newtown, is part of a scheme to encourage young growers to supply fresh produce to nearby towns and cities and boost domestic production in the face of increasing risks to national food supplies . The 15-hectare (36-acre) site is divided into three plots, each with a holiday chalet where the growers live, as well as shared facilities including a barn and diesel generator, to cover any power not provided by the farm’s solar panels. Gomersall’s farm, Cân y Pridd (Welsh for Song of the Soil), totals 4.9 hectares but she is now only growing on half a hectare, including in polytunnels, where she says she is “producing very big volumes for the scale”. She and her two neighbours are already providing fresh fruit and vegetables for the local community, through a veg box subscription service and at markets. In late July, they also started supplying fresh produce to Birmingham city council, where it is distributed to holiday clubs, giving disadvantaged children a taste of homegrown veg for perhaps the first time. The Wern farm project was launched by Our Food Trust, a charity which is working to increase levels of homegrown produce and aims to tackle Britain’s food insecurity . The UK depends on imports for about 40% of its food and has one of the lowest food self-sufficiency ratios among large western European countries, leaving it exposed to supply shocks prompted by the climate crisis, or other risks including geopolitical tensions and cyber-attacks. Just 0.2% of land in Wales is used for horticulture, according to the charity, giving huge scope for expansion. “We have to produce a lot more food for the regional and local market and for our cities,” says Duncan Fisher, joint chief executive at the charity. One way to do this is to remove barriers for young people who want to get into growing, Fisher says, but who often find themselves priced out of renting or buying land and a suitable home. “There are lots of well-trained and skilful growers who can’t find land to grow food on,” he says. “The price of land here is set by the market, by people who are not going to farm it.” The charity has given Gomersall the chance to turn a dream into reality and start a farm just 10 miles from where she grew up, while her neighbour, Lydia Dibben, says she was “quite blown away by the opportunity”. “It was amazing to be offered seven acres, which is a big amount for small-scale vegetable production, with a house with affordable rent and shared infrastructure,” says Dibben, 28. She and her partner Charlie James have named their plot Tir a Nant (Land and Stream). Our Food worked with the landowner, Powys county council, on the project, securing a 95-year lease for the plot and changes to the county’s planning guidance for rural enterprise dwellings, to enable growers to have a home on the land they work. The council leader, Jake Berriman, says “there was a perception that planning was a barrier and we wanted to remove that barrier”. He says local worries about extreme weather had also encouraged the authority to get involved. “We are starting to see genuine concern,” he says. “We have gone from flood to drought to fire.” The charity also negotiated the contract for the farmers to supply Birmingham, which has two aims: to give the growers a guaranteed buyer for some produce as they find their feet, while ensuring nutritious and sustainably produced fruit and vegetables reach deprived areas. The farmers have 35 customers for their veg box subscription service, along with selling to a local wholesaler and at regional markets. While they stress the importance of growing for their community, they do not believe that doing so would currently sustain their businesses. “Because of the cost of living crisis, there’s a limited amount of people who can afford to buy the veg we produce, and we are growing a hell of lot more than we can sell locally,” says Dibben, adding it was “really amazing being able to sell a hundred kilos of courgettes a week” to Birmingham.

events.title: Up 3,600%, this freight fund has posted the biggest gains of all on Iran war oil shock
events.summary: The Breakwave Tanker Shipping ETF (BWET) is up over 3,600% year to date, according to Morningstar, by far the best performance of any non-levered U.S. fund as the price of transporting oil has soared due to geopolitical shocks. Led by the U.S.-Iran war repercussions, there have been over 140,000 disrupted freight cargo vessels across the globe contributing to higher shipping rates. Experts see no quick end in sight especially after the Houthis took control of another key Red Sea oil choke point last week, but any fund that goes up this much is also prone to swift and severe reversals. As investors hunt for investment gains across the globe and diverse asset classes, from U.S. AI stocks to inflation hedges and crude oil contracts, something more mundane operating in the shadows of the global economy has racked up the biggest gains of all: freight tankers. The Breakwave Tanker Shipping ETF ( BWET ), which tracks the price of shipping oil , is up roughly 3,600% year-to-date as of early September, according to Morningstar data through Sept. 11, making it the best-performing non-levered fund in the U.S., as the U.S.-Iran conflict squeezes tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz turning a once-obscure freight investment into one of Wall Street's best trades. Supply chain and shipping routes will likely be further scrambled by Iran-backed Houthi rebels taking control of Yemen's key seaport of Mocka last week, a spot which allow the militia to wreak havoc with Red Sea shipping. The Red Sea had been used as an "alternate" to the perilous Persian Gulf. Further north on the peninsula, Saudi Arabian officials ordered a shut down of the kingdom's crucial East-West crude oil pipeline last week as a precautionary measure after multiple attacks by drones launched from Iraq. John Murillo, chief business officer of B2BROKER, which offers trading infrastructure technology to financial institutions, said the most important detail about BWET is that it tracks the price of shipping oil, rather than underlying crude oil prices . It is the only ETF to track the future cost of transporting crude oil, offering investors exposure to oil tanker futures without having to trade in the futures market directly. "It has very little to do with the oil price itself or its actual volume and depends mainly on geopolitics," Murillo said. Investors buying this fund are making a bet on how expensive it will be to move a barrel from the Middle East to consumers, he said, "and it became very expensive to do so after the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz began," he added. Year over year, rates on the Middle East oil tanker routes it tracks are up close to 500%, according to BWET's most recent biweekly tanker report on Sept. 8. As the hostilities continue, and difficulties persist passing through the Strait and the new choke points appear, many shipping companies have decided to avoid the region altogether, which makes trade routes longer and more expensive. With supertanker rates at record highs, shipping companies are making record profits. "This explains the fund's sheer growth and also points to the risk," Murillo said. But the risk of a swift and severe reversal doesn't look to be happening anytime soon, said Kyle Peacock, principal at Peacock Tariff Consulting, a tariff and customs advisory firm. He said it is not just the Iran war that has caused this freight trade to boom. Scrambling of traditional trade routes due to tariffs and widespread drought, with low water levels plaguing ports in Panama and in Europe leaving ships stranded , have created an unprecedented shortage of ships. "Companies are jumping at prices that might be 300 percent higher than they were paying, but that is the only ship available," Peacock said. "The shipping companies may have to route a ship farther, but their income is increasing tenfold," he said, as freight customers that have to move their goods drive up the prices as they compete for very limited space. Tariffs have also caused ships to be rerouted to destinations not typically served as heavily. One of Peacock's clients moved a manufacturing facility from China to Hungary to avoid tariffs. "These new trade routes are taking from the supply of vessels," Peacock said. In typical freight times, the container ship companies dictate the routes, but right now, urgency in the market is leading routes to be determined by the highest bidder, Peacock said. "Long-time clients are being bumped from carriers for the highest bidder," he said. "It is at a tipping point, because what trade route is now more profitable is how carriers are looking at it ... backwards from the way it was in the past," he added. events.title: My 19-year-old moved across the country with 4 days' notice. What he packed made it easier to let him go.
events.summary: The author's son (not pictured) brought his teddy with him when he went to college. FatCamera/Getty Images My oldest son told me on a Monday that he was moving 3,000 miles away that Thursday. I understood his need to leave because I'd made a similar move at the same age. When I visited his new home, I discovered he'd brought the Christmas bear he'd had since childhood. My oldest son was my only child for three years. I think that built a bond that doesn't exist with any of his four siblings who had to share me from day one with an expanding brood of children. I can honestly say, I do not have a favorite child , but it was this oldest one who taught me how to be a mother. That included how to let go when the time came. At the age of 19 after an inauspicious start to college, he moved cross-country to San Francisco, a frequent transition for kids who grow up in Boston. Since he was the first of my five to depart home, it hit me pretty hard; but it was clear he needed a change and I willingly co-signed his decision. I did the same thing at the same age My son informed me of his impending move on a Monday. He left that Thursday. I didn't discourage him. I'd done the same thing at the same age. Like him, I'd notified my mother that I was leaving home just four days before I actually did. My destination was Phoenix, where I was joining my brother who'd just moved west to accept a job in the desert and had invited me to join him. I packed my most important worldly possessions in a camp trunk, shipped it out first and then flew to our new home. The author's kids all moved away from her. Courtesy of the author My son was riding across the country in a van with three other 19-year-olds. He packed even less than me. I don't remember crying as I watched them depart. I was already thinking about the mess he'd left behind and how it was up to me to clean it up. I braced myself for what I was about to find Our house was small and with so many children, we'd converted almost every inch of living space into a bedroom. My son's room had been our basement playroom, but when he hit puberty, I wanted him to have privacy away from his younger siblings so sent him downstairs to his own personal lair. His brother, who still shared a room with two siblings, coveted the space and didn't take long to box up his belongings in anticipation of a move downstairs. Before he could haul his things down, though, I wanted to clear out whatever might have been left behind. I was nervous about what I might find and didn't want any of the other kids to uncover something illicit or illegal. The author's oldest son taught her how to let go. Courtesy of the author Fortunately, I didn't find any contraband although I wondered what might be in the small safe in the closet. When I asked him, my son said it was empty and since he'd lost the key and we couldn't open it I decided to accept that answer. There were a few books and some out-of-date electronics, but most of what he left behind were clothes he'd outgrown. I wasn't surprised when I found a Playboy magazine hidden under a pile of old sweaters. In fact, it made me laugh as I recalled my parents finding an issue when my brother left home. It's what he took with him that surprised me the most The clear-out didn't take long. If he could be unsentimental about what he'd left behind, so could I. By the end of the day, his brother had taken over the space, made it his own, and settled in. The intrepid travelers arrived safely on the West Coast five days later. They easily found jobs and a place to live. My son's first job in the Bay Area was on an assembly line in an electronics factory. It was an enlightening experience for him that empowered his next decision — registering for college and setting forth on the path towards the career he has today. The author's son took his teddy bear to college. Courtesy of the author When he moved into his own apartment, I went out to help him set it up. He gave me a tour of the space and proudly commented on how he wanted to fix it up. As I stepped into his bedroom, I saw something familiar propped up on his mattress. It was his Christmas bear that had sat under our tree each year since toddlerhood. I hadn't realized he'd taken this childhood treasure with him. My oldest moving out was the first monumental shift in our family dynamic. When I looked at that stuffed bear, I knew that even though he now lived 3000 miles away from me, my son really wasn't that far from home. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Dario Amodei says OpenAI's Hugging Face hack helped convince him AI needs to slow down
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says AI development needs to slow down. Andrej Sokolow/picture alliance via Getty Images Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says he's now 'convinced' AI development needs to slow down. Amodei cited OpenAI agents' Hugging Face hack as one reason. The Anthropic CEO proposed a three-step plan for the AI industry to slow things down. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says he's "become convinced" in recent months that AI needs to slow down. And rogue OpenAI agents are part of the reason. Amodei cited the July Hugging Face breach,  in which OpenAI agents broke out of their testing environment to hack into the AI platform and then hide their tracks, as one of the catalysts for his heightened alarm. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet," he wrote in a blog post published Saturday. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Saturday that he agreed with Amodei. "We need to pace the frontier," he said on X. "This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks." Elon Musk, whose SpaceXAI competes with Anthropic and OpenAI, also backed Amodei's proposition on Saturday, writing in an X post, "Dario is right." Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google's AI program, DeepMind, said on X that "Dario's essay points towards the right path forward." He reminded everyone that two months ago, he outlined his own vision for how AI should be developed and governed. Amodei also cited the rapid advancement of AI in recent months and its increased capacity for "recursive self-improvement," which is essentially an AI model's ability to learn on its own. Amodei proposed a three-step plan to slow down AI development to ensure the tech's safety "while still achieving its benefits and grappling with important geopolitical dilemmas." Central to Amodei's plan is embedding independent safety evaluators inside frontier AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, giving them "employee-like access" to the companies' systems and work. "This is the key step for verifiability of any pacing commitments," Amodei wrote. "Anthropic is unilaterally committing to this step now." In his X post, Altman said OpenAI would also implement third-party evaluators into its company. "We'll have more to share soon," he said. The AI community has been in a furor this week after Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon quit, issuing a public warning that AI agents could "kill us all by the end of the decade." Coxon's warnings were shared widely and signal-boosted by other Anthropic employees, one of whom, the company's alignment science lead, said on X, "Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" On Saturday, Coxon reposted Musk's "Dario is right" post. Earlier in the week, Musk accused Coxon of orchestrating a "setup." OpenAI's chief scientist, meanwhile, also said in a blog post last week that leading AI labs need to coordinate a slowdown . "No one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," Jakub Pachocki said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman reposted Pachocki's comments on X, calling it an "important post." Bloomberg reported this week that, during an employee meeting, Altman said OpenAI was willing to slow AI development in conjunction with rival labs. In his Saturday essay, Amodei reiterated previous calls for the US government to intervene and establish guidelines for American labs. The Trump administration, so far, has resisted regulating the American AI industry to maintain its narrowing lead over Chinese AI labs. Democratic lawmakers, for their part, proposed stringent legislation this week that would severely hamper AI development. Sen. Bernie Sanders, in a recent interview with MSNOW, said AI companies "need to stop right now." Amodei and other leading AI researchers and engineers have not argued for a full stop to development. In his essay, Amodei said American AI labs should continue developing, just with more robust safeguards. He said there remains a need to compete with China, and said the Trump administration could ensure this by not selling the rival the advanced chips needed to power AI models. "The stakes are too high for pacing to be an empty exercise — we need to use the time it gives us wisely," Amodei said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The 19 actors with the most Emmy wins of all time
events.summary: Mary Tyler Moore won seven Emmys. Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images The Emmys are pretty much the Oscars for television. We compiled a list of actors with the most Emmys, from Mary Tyler Moore to Bryan Cranston. The 2026 Emmy Awards will air on Monday, September 14, on NBC and Peacock. An Emmy is the biggest award an actor can win for their work on the small screen — and when there's a show or a performance Emmy voters love, it often gets multiple nominations and wins. We've pored over the stats and compiled a list of the most Emmy-awarded actors of all time. It includes some of the biggest TV stars of all time, including Bryan Cranston , Betty White, Mary Tyler Moore, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus. In fact, Louis-Dreyfus is tied with Cloris Leachman for eight Emmy wins as a performer and with Carl Reiner for the most total Emmy wins among the actors on this list, with 11, if you include their awards in other categories, too. The total Emmy wins listed here aren't exclusively for performances: Some on this list have won for writing, directing, or producing — Cranston was a producer on "Breaking Bad," and Louis-Dreyfus is an executive producer for " Veep ," for example — but the majority of their Emmys are for acting.  Here are the actors with the most Emmy wins. Fox — 5 wins and 19 nominations Michael J. Fox at the 2000 Emmy Awards. Bob Riha Jr/Getty Images Fox won three consecutive Emmys in '86, '87, and '88 for playing Alex P. Keaton in "Family Ties." He won another two for "Spin City" and "Rescue Me." In 2026, he was nominated for his guest appearance on "Shrinking," but lost to Rob Reiner, who won posthumously for his appearance on "The Bear." 11 (tie). Art Carney — 6 wins and 12 nominations Art Carney and one of his Emmy Awards. NBC/NBCUniversal/Getty Images Carney won four times for "The Jackie Gleason Show," once for "The Honeymooners," and once for the made-for-TV film "Terrible Joe Moran." 8 (tie). Tyne Daly — 6 wins and 16 nominations Tyne Daly at the 1996 Emmy Awards. events.title: Fusion power startups find new partners in the defense world
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Fusion power is getting back to its roots. As fusion startups keep chasing their ultimate goal — putting electrons on the grid — many are also now embracing, or returning to, the defense applications that laid the foundation for the industry. The sector emerged decades ago when physicists looked for more constructive uses of the science behind the thermonuclear bombs that proliferated during the Cold War. The national security angle never really went away. A groundbreaking fusion power experiment in 2022 happened at the National Ignition Facility, which has supported national security applications for more than 25 years. That shift has accelerated as venture dollars committed to climate tech — the funds that typically have supported fusion startups — have stalled . Fusion startups have captured a large portion of recent climate tech funding, but fusion is an expensive business, and VCs are always happy when their portfolio companies find other sources of money. That’s where the defense industry comes in. The defense industry has explored laser weapons for years, but interest has spiked as drones have reshaped modern warfare. Traditional air defense systems were designed to target human-piloted aircraft, which tend to be larger and fewer in number. That has led to some comical mismatches between aggressor and defender. For example, about a decade ago, a U.S. ally used a $3 million Patriot missile to shoot down a $200 consumer drone. Effective, but not very efficient. Laser weapons promise to alter the math. Instead of firing a single, expensive, one-use missile per shot, they fire quickly and relatively cheaply, using electricity drawn from a generator or a ship’s reactor or engine. Fusion startups working on laser-based reactor designs are ideal partners in developing such weapons. Last week, laser-based fusion startup Xcimer announced a partnership with and investment from RTX, the conglomerate that includes defense contractor Raytheon. Under the deal, Xcimer gets funding from RTX Ventures, while RTX can start exploring how to use Xcimer’s powerful lasers for its own purposes. Denver-based Xcimer currently operates what it says is the largest privately owned laser system in the world, which it plans to use to develop a power plant. Inside its power plant, lasers will bombard fuel targets, compressing them until the atoms inside fuse and release energy. The startup’s current laser system, Phoenix, operates at an order of magnitude lower power than will be required for a power plant, but it is powerful enough to have caught the attention of the defense industry. Xcimer isn’t the only player in the defense space. Pacific Fusion announced a memorandum of understanding last month with the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) to work together on high-energy-density fusion experiments. The startup recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico not far from the Sandia and Los Alamos National Laboratories. While its primary purpose is to demonstrate that the company’s design can generate more power than the facility consumes, it has other uses. The fusion reactions at Pacific Fusion’s facility will be far more powerful than those the government currently uses to perform nuclear weapons experiments. “It turns out that the facility that we’re building also has utility in this world-leading defense application,” Keith LeChein, co-founder and chief technical officer at Pacific Fusion, told TechCrunch recently. It might sound like a convenient coincidence, but it isn’t one. Defense applications were “always on our mind,” said Carrie von Muench, co-founder and chief operating officer at Pacific Fusion. LeChien, who developed the company’s core technology, previously worked at Sandia National Laboratories, the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, and the National Nuclear Security Administration. Fusion power has come a long way since the first weapons scientists dreamt it up decades ago, but its national security applications haven’t been forgotten. Their recent reacquaintance is perhaps overdue, and promises to give willing fusion startups a helpful boost. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism.

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Ingenious coders coaxed multichannel chiptunes from the humblest of sound hardware Digital Research's GEM opens a new window on Linux 2 days ago Retired man turns spare room into Soviet-era supercomputer 5 days ago On Call: Exec couldn’t identify a photocopier, which made for a fax-inating tech support call 16 days ago AROS, the FOSS recreation of AmigaOS, comes to Raspberry Pi 17 days ago Agents made my retro tech safe to use again and showed their real value as testers of ideas August 12, 2026 Even for 1982, the Sinclair ZX Spectrum had poor sound: a piezoelectric speaker that could beep. But you can do a lot with a single bit if you turn it on and off really fast. Michael Martin's Bumbershoot Software site has done some fascinating deep dives into several long-gone computer systems, including a whole series on implementing a game on the ZX Spectrum, starting in May with Giving the ZX Spectrum a Fair Shake . More recently, though, Martin turned his attention to the Spectrum's very limited sound capabilities. As we write, his newest post is Experimenting With 1-Bit Sound . The post concerns the original 16K and 48K ZX Spectrum models, not the Spectrum 128, with its fancy AY-3-8912 sound chip (also found in the US Timex Sinclair 2068). Even as devoted Spectrum enthusiasts, we didn't expect an article about the machine's limited sound hardware to lead to hours of listening pleasure. The Manic Miner intro music , after all, is a fair representation of early Spectrum chiptunes. (Turn your speakers way down before you listen!) The ZX Spectrum could play music from the outset – Steven Vickers' original Spectrum BASIC Manual includes the code for a tiny fragment of Mahler . As The Register reported in 2015 , Matt Westcott's Mahler Project used a networked collection of original Spectrum computers to play all the parts of Mahler's First Symphony. Over at Bumbershoot Software, Martin is interested in programming the very limited hardware of these early home computers, and so his Spectrum audio post discusses audio-encoding methods, pulse-width modulation, and more in considerable depth. Toward the end, it links to a remarkable music demo called We are Vocoders . A discussion among Spectrum aficionados on Hacker News then led us to the astounding work of Tim Follin in the 1980s. (The Video Game Music Preservation Foundation has an excellent profile , including a contemporary photo. Dean Belfield's touching tribute to his brother Geoff has a more recent picture.) Follin hand-coded the music for Spectrum games such as Mastertronic's Agent X … There are many more remarkable Follin tracks, including the music for Future Games , and the title music for Chronos . Follin achieved this without additional hardware such as the RAM Music Machine – which even impressed the great Aphex Twin . There are also some very impressive demos, such as Dark Fusion by the late Ben Daglish . Rich "Tufty" Hollins even created an entire half-hour album of one-bit audio, ON and OFF . You can listen to it in its entirety on Bandcamp , or accompanied by some Spec-tastic graphics on YouTube . ® Who, Me?

events.title: AI's most powerful CEOs hit the brakes
events.summary: In nine startling hours on Saturday, the four biggest AI labs — which rarely agree on anything — set aside years of feuds and competition to endorse a slower development pace for their models. Their new stance: Prioritize safety over growth , even at a cost. The big picture: AI's unrelenting growth has hit an inflection point with the public, Washington and even the companies building it. Data centers are unpopular . People are panicked about doom scenarios . And 51 days before midterms, legislators suddenly realize there are points to be won by cracking down. Against that backdrop , the industry's most powerful CEOs hit the brakes Saturday. At 10 a.m. ET, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei dropped a 3,800-word essay saying model development needs to be paced , otherwise doom scenarios are possible — like a rogue-agent takeover of the entire internet, which he said could be as soon as six months from now. An hour later, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shocked the AI chattering class by quoting Amodei's essay on X and saying "Dario is right." Musk — who heads SpaceXAI, formerly xAI — had pointedly not joined previous industry-wide calls for any kind of slowdown. At 12:30 p.m., OpenAI CEO Sam Altman tweeted: "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier." In an interview Friday that was released on Saturday, Altman told Fortune his company won't go public this year, dashing hopes for a blockbuster IPO. He said OpenAI has too much safety work to do and would be better off doing that as a private company. At 7 p.m., Demis Hassabis — the Nobel laureate who co-founded and chairs Google DeepMind, and is Alphabet's chief scientist — tweeted : "Dario's essay points towards the right path forward. The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment." Between the lines: Publicly putting safety ahead of technological or financial growth may be the industry's only route to avoid a crackdown that's not on its terms. Legislators are begging House Speaker Mike Johnson to stay in session and do something about the "threat" of AI. The more extreme alternative is something like Sen. Bernie Sanders' push to force a pause and make the most advanced AI illegal. Reality check: Most people realize there's too much money at stake to just stop moving forward. But the tradeoff may be between historic riches and slightly less historic riches. Let's see whether they actually agree on what oversight ("embedded third-party evaluators") and "slow" mean, then follow through Friction point: No one in China is having the same kind of we'd-better-stop moment. Influential Silicon Valley tech voices, including former Trump official David Sacks, spent Saturday highlighting the counterargument that slowing down just lets adversaries — with no such safety qualms — catch up. In a late Saturday-night post , Sacks effectively dared OpenAI and Anthropic to voluntarily pace the AI frontier without waiting for the government. "If you don't, we'll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop." Amodei even acknowledged that a safety regime only really works if authoritarian governments come to the table, too. "Pacing within democracies will be limited by the lead that U.S. companies have over authoritarian regimes, chiefly the Chinese Communist Party," he wrote . "If we slow down by more than this amount, then (unpaced) CCP-associated projects will pull ahead, creating significant national security risk." The bottom line: Saturday may go down as the day AI changed — when industry moguls vowed to limit themselves. Read Amodei's essay , "We Must Pace the Frontier."

events.title: I travel often, but just took my first luxury cruise. The food was great, and it was easy to relax, but there was 1 unexpected drawback.
events.summary: The author went on her first cruise at 49. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin Though I travel often, I had never been on a cruise. I had misconceptions about this popular way of travel. All that changed when my husband and I went on a luxury cruise for my 49th birthday. Even as a seasoned traveler , it took me nearly five decades to get on a cruise ship at all. I had never been particularly curious about cruising and had some pretty unflattering ideas about what it involved: heaping buffets of dubious food, brightly colored drinks, crowded decks, and a style of travel that seemed much too packaged for me. Then, this summer, I spent nine nights traveling through Northern Europe and discovered that much of what I thought I knew about cruising was wrong. My husband and I went on a cruise for my 49th birthday. The author realized she had some misconceptions about cruises. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin My husband and I sailed aboard Crystal Serenity from Southampton to Copenhagen, a voyage on which I would celebrate my 49th birthday. And this was admittedly a very cushy introduction: I stayed in a Sapphire Veranda Suite with a walk-in closet, veranda, and butler service. So I'm certainly not suggesting my experience represents every cruise. But as someone who typically takes complicated, high-effort trips, I found these were the things that surprised me most about my first one. I couldn't believe how easy everything was. Planning a cruise was much easier than the author's typical way of traveling. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin I'm accustomed to doing a lot of work when I travel. I tend to build ambitious itineraries involving multiple cities, hotels, trains, flights, restaurant reservations, and activities. I love that kind of travel, but there are a lot of logistics involved — and as the mom and travel planner in chief, I'm usually the one managing them all. Cruising took an astonishing amount of that effort away. I unpacked once, put everything in the closet, slid my empty suitcase under the bed, and didn't deal with it again for nine nights. While I slept, ate dinner, or watched a show, my hotel was effortlessly transporting me to another country. The rest felt similarly organized. An on-ship newsletter featured printed itineraries that told me exactly what would be happening on board the following day. Excursions were coordinated around the ship's arrival and departure. Restaurants, entertainment, and activities were steps from my room. I hadn't realized just how much mental and physical energy I normally spend administering my own trips until I didn't have to. The food was incredible. They were pleasantly surprised by the food on the cruise. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin Cruise food , in my imagination, was mostly about quantity: enormous buffets of mediocre food feeding thousands of people at once. What I encountered on Crystal was very different. The main dining room didn't repeat dishes, so you could always count on something new to try. Beyond that, my favorite meals came from places that I'd consider hot restaurants even in my buzzy hometown of Los Angeles. Umi Uma, created by Nobu Matsuhisa, served sophisticated Japanese food and sushi. Osteria d'Ovidio offered seriously high-end Italian cooking. Obviously, this was a luxury ship , and I wouldn't assume every cruise serves food like this one did. But it thoroughly dismantled my assumption that cruise dining necessarily meant choosing among endless ho-hum chafing dishes at a buffet. I couldn't believe I sometimes preferred staying on board to sightseeing. The author was surprised that sometimes, she wanted to stay on board instead of going on excursions. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin Before this trip, I couldn't understand why anyone would travel somewhere only to spend the day on a ship. But the ship turned me into such a person. There were history lectures, art classes, live performances, a spa, pools, a movie theater, and a casino. I entered a $100 blackjack tournament on a whim and somehow came in third (I'll be getting mileage out of this proud moment for years to come). The ultimate test came when we docked in Rotterdam. We had booked an excursion to Amsterdam that would take most of the day, but we decided to cancel it to spend more time on board. I never would have seen that coming. I actually relaxed — something I'm not very good at doing on trips. Traveling by cruise offered a nice change of pace. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin I love travel, but my tendency to cram a lot into every trip means I frequently return home exhausted. On the cruise, I slept like an absolute baby. (My husband suggested it might be the gentle motion of the sea that lulled me.) In fact, I slept in so late that I ended up setting my alarm for 10 a.m. I knew I'd miss regular breakfast, but I didn't want to miss the late-riser breakfast from 10 to 11 — or sleep through a day when there were things on board I actually wanted to do. Without transportation to arrange, hotels to change, or a packed sightseeing agenda to manage, I settled into a pace I rarely allow myself while traveling. For once, the words "travel" and "vacation" actually felt synonymous. I sometimes questioned how deeply I was experiencing the destinations. However, sometimes she felt she wasn't truly experiencing the places they docked. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin For all the things I loved about cruising, one of my original reservations did bear out. I usually think of travel as a way to experience a place and its culture. I like wandering neighborhoods, eating local cuisine, figuring out public transportation , and having the kinds of unplanned interactions that happen when you're actually immersed in a destination (even when they're stressful). A port stop is different. We visited some incredible places, and we were generally there for only a few hours before returning to the ship. There was less time for wandering, spontaneity, or meaningful cultural exchange. In that sense, this cruise felt more like a true vacation than the kind of travel I typically do. And, as it turns out, I really needed and enjoyed that. But I did sometimes wonder how much I could say I'd truly experienced a destination after seeing it within the relatively controlled framework of a port day. So if my primary goal were to deeply get to know a place, I'd still choose to stay there rather than visit it by ship. But I loved the shipboard experience, and it turned out to be one of the best trips I've taken in recent memory. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Surging inflation puts interest rates back in focus as policymakers meet in Japan, US and UK
events.summary: Iran war and turbulent global bond markets add to pressure as rate decisions loom this week in major western economies Economics viewpoint: perilous UK economic conditions trace back to Trump Central bankers in economies including the US, Japan and the UK will face a moment of truth this week, as surging inflation raises the prospect of higher interest rates. Policymakers in all three countries will set rates in the next seven days against the backdrop of turbulent global bond markets . In particular, investors will be watching closely to see if Kevin Warsh, the new chair of the US Federal Reserve , can face down Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts and instead persuade Fed governors to raise them on Wednesday. Warsh was handpicked by the US president , who has repeatedly demanded lower interest rates. In a Truth Social post this month, Trump claimed the US should have the “LOWEST RATE of any country in the World”. He added: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.” However, the central bank’s board of governors is having to contend with a renewed rise in oil prices after the US-Iran conflict intensified again . The cost of a barrel of crude surged past $100 last week for the first time since July, as the strait of Hormuz remained all but closed to tanker traffic and Houthi rebels advanced along the Red Sea coast, threatening to choke off Saudi oil supplies. Oil prices eased slightly on Friday amid hopes of fresh talks to reopen the waterway but remained well above levels in the summer, when Middle East hostilities temporarily abated. Higher energy costs are expected to feed a fresh rise in US inflation, which has been above the Fed’s 2% target for more than five years. In a speech this month, Warsh said without continued progress towards the target, Fed policymakers would have “work to do”. Data published on Friday showed annual US inflation unchanged at 3.4%. Andrew Bailey, the Bank of England governor, has struck a calm note about above-target inflation in the UK, saying rising mortgage rates have done some of the work of a rate rise without the Bank taking action. Markets and economists are predicting the Bank will hold rates at 3.75% on Thursday. However, three of the nine members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for a rate rise in July , and data published on Friday showing stronger-than-expected economic growth could amplify fears about inflation. Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at RSM, a consultancy firm, said the latest rise in energy prices had “materially increased the chance that the MPC will eventually follow other major central banks and raise rates”. But he predicted a “hawkish hold” from the Bank when the MPC convenes on Thursday: a decision to leave rates unchanged, but with the published minutes pointing to potential future rises. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Financial markets are betting on four UK rate rises over the next 12 months – up from the three they were expecting before the latest surge in oil prices. In Tokyo, Bank of Japan (BoJ) policymakers will announce their decision on Friday and are widely expected to raise interest rates, validating the recent recovery of the yen on foreign exchanges. A quarter-point increase in the BoJ’s policy rate, to 1.25%, would take it to levels not seen for more than 30 years, since Japan first began fighting an extended battle against deflation, or falling prices. The US Treasury joined Japanese authorities in intervening in foreign exchange markets to support the yen in July and Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, has made it clear that he expects rates to rise. At an event at Southern Methodist University in Texas on Tuesday, Bessent said: “When we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do. I have asymmetric information. I am the house now. You can bet against me if you want.” The European Central Bank raised interest rates on Thursday . Christine Lagarde, its president, said: “The conflict in the Middle ​East continues ​to ⁠generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to ​remain well above target for ​an ⁠extended period.”
